prose.intro: Every controller on this page is judged on the same eight held-out weeks, against the same reference (doing nothing, or the thermostat on S3), and next to the exact optimum with perfect foresight, which no real controller can reach.
findings:
Reinforcement learning did not beat the reference on any rung. The central learner saves -1.1 % (S1), -3.0 % (S2) and -59.5 % (S3) of the bill, where a negative number is a loss; on S3 it also lets the buildings get cold.
A planner that re-solves the optimisation every hour with the true future reaches the ideal saving: 14.6 % on S2 against a ceiling of 14.6 %. The gap to the ceiling is therefore the cost of not knowing the future, not of the method.
With forecasts that use the weather the same planner reaches 3.4 % (S1), 8.8 % (S2) and 11.4 % (S3), against -0.2 %, 5.6 % and 6.0 % for the hand-set solar rule. That is 61 % and 77 % of the ceiling on S2 and S3. The weather is taken as known in these runs.
Forecasts that only look at the past are not enough: copying the same hour of last week gives 3.7 % on S2, less than the solar rule.
The household load is the forecast that limits everything. With the true load instead of a forecast the S2 saving rises from 8.8 % to 12.5 %. The load of these buildings is a constructed composite, so this limit may differ for real houses.
The planner that only minimises the bill raises the highest hour of the district from 66 kW to 117 kW. A small peak weight keeps the saving (8.9 %) and brings the highest hour to 63 kW.
On S3, if the planner's room model is wrong by a fifth, comfort is violated for 396 K·h over the eight weeks. Online correction of the model plus a small comfort margin brings that to 0 K·h at a saving of 10.6 %.
Planning against error scenarios of the measured size did worse than planning against one forecast (4.3 % to 7.6 % against 9.0 %). The cause is not identified.
prose.rl_note: The learners were trained for a short budget with a reward whose weights were set by hand and not tuned. This is a negative result for these settings, not a proof that learning cannot work here.
prose.forecast_note: Error is expressed as a multiple of the standard deviation of each series. The synthetic points add that much random error to the true future. The two real forecasters are placed by their measured error on the eight test weeks: the household load, the forecast that limits everything, is off by 0.89 for the history-only forecaster and 0.68 for the weather-conditioned one; the solar forecast is off by 0.60 and 0.07. The weather is taken as known in the weather-conditioned case, so its solar error is a lower bound.
prose.tradeoff_note: Each point is one peak weight in the planner. The weight is a tuning knob in the optimisation, not a tariff. The highest hour is the largest district grid draw in the eight test weeks.
prose.model_error_note: The planner believes the building has a different heat loss and heat capacity than the simulated one. Comfort is the sum of temperature shortfalls below the setpoint over all buildings and hours, in kelvin-hours.
prose.curves_note: Bill change against the reference during training, evaluated on the test weeks; a positive number is a loss. Each line is one training run.
prose.stochastic_note: Several error scenarios per decision, with the first steps shared by all scenarios. At the measured error size every variant is worse than the single forecast; with the sampled errors scaled down to a fraction the result returns to the single-forecast level.
